content.text: I confirmed the delay in personal builds #148 and #149: staging took about 5½ minutes, followed by another 6 minutes in `archiveArtifacts`. Build #149 archived 88,740 files totaling 10.43 GiB; roughly 98% of the bytes are `.gkyl` outputs. The staging code launches separate `dirname`, `mkdir`, and `cp` commands for each file, so there are two substantial costs to address.

The delay is real: **the personal pipeline copies and archives about 10 GiB across 89,000 files per build.**

I inspected the local Jenkins records:

| Operation | Build #148 | Build #149 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Stage files into the workspace | 5m 37s | 5m 22s |
| Jenkins `archiveArtifacts` | 6m 04s | 5m 58s |
| Combined | **11m 41s** | **11m 20s** |

Build #149 archived **88,740 files / 10.43 GiB**, split almost equally between candidate and baseline results. About **98% of the bytes are `.gkyl` outputs**.

Two things make this expensive:

- [The staging helper](/var/home/mrosen/gkeyll/ci/jenkins/baseline_cache.sh:291) runs separate `dirname`, `mkdir`, and `cp` commands **for every file**. It copies both result trees into the workspace, then copies the baseline again into the retained run directory.
- [The personal Jenkinsfile](/var/home/mrosen/gkeyll/ci/jenkins/jenkinsfile.personal:714) archives both complete trees, including on successful runs and baseline cache hits. Jenkins’ default artifact manager transfers files through its agent connection using gzip compression and stores them on the controller. That adds compression, transfer, and filesystem work. [Jenkins implementation](https://github.com/jenkinsci/jenkins/blob/master/core/src/main/java/jenkins/model/StandardArtifactManager.java)

I recommend these changes, in order:

1. **Replace per-file shell copying with a bulk copy operation.** Preserve the existing regular-file-only selection and paths. This targets the first five minutes without changing what users can download.
2. **Package numerical outputs into a few archives directly from the retained result trees.** Use fast compression, such as low-level zstd. Keep reports, logs, configs, and regression databases individually accessible. This avoids staging thousands of loose output files and recreating them on the controller; individual `.gkyl` downloads would require extraction.
3. **Optionally make full numerical-output archival opt-in.** Routine builds could archive diagnostics and failing-test outputs, while retaining complete data in the existing run directory. This offers the largest reduction, but changes what remains downloadable through Jenkins.

**I’d start with bulk staging and packaged outputs**, preserving all results. The timings establish where the time goes; the speedup still needs measurement after those changes. No configuration or files were changed.
Implement 1 and 2 1. Replace per-file shell copying with a bulk copy operation 2. Package numerical outputs into a few archives directly from the retained result trees

I’ll replace the per-file staging loops with bulk copying and package numerical outputs directly from the retained result trees. Reports, logs, configs, and regression databases will remain individually downloadable. I’ll also update the artifact rules and retrieval documentation, then run the CI helper tests.

I’ll create one numerical-output archive for the candidate and one for the baseline, using fast zstd compression when available and gzip otherwise. Non-numerical files will keep their existing download paths, and the retained run directory will still contain the full unpacked results. I’m using the testing-and-verification skill to check archive round-trips, symlink handling, and the existing cache lifecycle.
